title: DnNP: Denoising Input Uncertainty in Neural Processes
claim: Standard models assume clean inputs; ours adds a latent denoising stage that recovers clean inputs before the usual encoder-decoder.
layout: 2x2 grid: baseline left, ours right; graphical model above, architecture below
description: A two-column, two-row comparison separated by dotted lines. The left column is labeled Neural Processes and the right column Denoising Neural Processes. The top row shows graphical models. Left: a latent z points to shaded observed nodes y_C, x_C (context box) and y_T, x_T (target box). Right: unshaded latent clean inputs x*_C and x*_T point to shaded noisy observations x_C and x_T. The bottom row shows architectures. Left: blue x_i,y_i boxes feed an orange Encoder trapezoid, then a gray z box, then an orange Decoder that outputs y_4. Right: the same pipeline with a green Denoiser block inserted first, which outputs x*_i before the encoder. The green block is the main focal point.
caption: Comparison of Neural Processes (NP) and DnNP in terms of graphical model (top) and architecture (bottom). In the graphical model, shaded nodes represent observed variables. Standard NPs assume that inputs are observed noise-free, an assumption violated in many real-world settings where measurements are inherently corrupted by noise. DnNP addresses this by treating noise-free inputs as latent variables x∗that must be inferred from noisy observations x, while preserving the standard NP structure of context and target sets with a global latent z that captures functionlevel uncertainty. In the architecture, DnNP extends the standard NP encoder-decoder pipeline by prepending a denoising component (shown in green) that recovers noise-free input estimates from noisy inputs before passing them to the encoder.
abstract: Neural Processes (NPs) are flexible meta-learning models capable of uncertainty quantification across diverse applications. However, the standard NP framework assumes access to noise-free inputs. This is unrealistic in many practical settings, where sensor noise or measurement errors are unavoidable. This discrepancy between model assumptions and real-world data can significantly degrade prediction quality and uncertainty estimates. We introduce Denoising Neural Processes (DnNPs), a principled extension of the NP framework that explicitly models input uncertainty. We train DnNPs via variational inference. DnNPs jointly learn to denoise corrupted inputs and perform meta-learning, making them robust to noisy training data. We demonstrate DnNPs' effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing consistent improvements in prediction and uncertainty quantification compared to standard NPs. On PM2.5 spatial interpolation from real-world air quality sensors, DnNP reduces RMSE by up to 30% and NLL by up to 73% relative to standard NPs. We also provide theoretical grounding: we show that the Bayes-optimal predictor under noisy inputs belongs to the DnNP model class, and that plug-in models with fixed observation variance incur an irreducible KL divergence gap that DnNP provably avoids.
